Nicolò Acciapacci (1383–1447) was a Neapolitan bishop and cardinal. An ally of Francesco Sforza, he spent his last years in exile from Rome, but was considered a candidate for the papacy in 1447.

As a member of the powerful Acciapacci family, Nicolò was born into a life of privilege and later became a key figure in the Italian Renaissance. He was appointed bishop of Vibo Valentia in 1414 and was elected cardinal in 1427, a position that gave him significant influence in the Vatican.

Nicolò's involvement with Francesco Sforza, the Duke of Milan, led to his own exile from Rome in the late 1440s. Despite this, he remained a strong candidate for the papacy in 1447, sparking a contentious papal election.

Nicolò Acciapacci's legacy is complex and multifaceted. His work as a bishop and cardinal helped shape the course of Italian politics and religion during the late Middle Ages. However, his involvement with the Sforza family also raises questions about the role of patronage and corruption in the Catholic Church.

The 12th of April 1447 marks the date of Nicolò Acciapacci's untimely death, a tragic end to a life that had been marked by both great achievement and controversy.

The significance of Nicolò Acciapacci lies in his role as a bridge between the medieval and early modern periods in Italy, a time of great upheaval and transformation.

The Acciapacci family's influence extended beyond Nicolò's own lifetime, with his descendants playing significant roles in Italian politics and society for centuries to come.

Nicolò Acciapacci's story is one of intrigue, power, and the complexities of human ambition.

Nicolò Acciapacci (1383–1447) was a Neapolitan bishop and cardinal who played a crucial role in the politics of the Holy Roman Empire during the 15th century. His involvement with the Medici family and his advocacy for the interests of the Italian city-states led to his exile from Rome in 1446. In the same year, he was appointed as the Bishop of Bari, a position he held until his death in 1447. Acciapacci's efforts to secure the papacy for his ally, Francesco Sforza, ultimately proved unsuccessful, but his legacy as a key figure in the politics of the Italian Renaissance endures.

Aciapacci was a key figure in the complex web of alliances and rivalries that characterized the politics of the Holy Roman Empire during the 15th century. His involvement with the Medici family, who were major patrons of the arts and architects of the Italian Renaissance, highlights the intersection of politics, culture, and religion in the Renaissance era. Acciapacci's role in the politics of the Italian city-states, particularly his advocacy for the interests of Naples and the papacy, had significant implications for the balance of power in Europe.

The legacy of Nicolò Acciapacci extends beyond his own lifetime, as his efforts to secure the papacy for his ally, Francesco Sforza, contributed to the rise of the Medici dynasty and the growth of the Catholic Church in Italy. His involvement in the politics of the Italian city-states also had significant implications for the development of the nation-state and the rise of modern nationhood. Acciapacci's legacy serves as a reminder of the complex and often fraught nature of politics in the Renaissance era, where the interests of powerful families and institutions often took precedence over the needs of the common people.
